unit.title: Perform oxyacetylene welding process (fuel gas) to AWS specification

summary: This unit is about oxyacetylene welding of carbon steel plate and small-bore pipe to an AWS specification: working to a written procedure (WPS), proving the procedure (PQR) and qualifying welders (WPQ). You will learn to set up to a WPS, choose and care for AWS-class gas welding rods, weld test coupons in the positions the code names, inspect and bend test them against the code's limits, and keep the records that make a qualification fair and traceable.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). In the AWS system, oxyacetylene welding is one kind of **oxyfuel gas welding (OFW)**. This unit is about OFW done **to specification**: every weld is made to a written procedure that has been proved by test, by a welder who has passed a test, and every step is recorded.

You will spend much of this unit on **test coupons**: short plate and pipe joints welded in set positions, then inspected and broken or bent to see what is inside. A coupon shows in an hour what a production weld might show only when it fails in service.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees who can already gas weld steel sheet and plate, and who will now weld to a procedure, take qualification tests, help to prove procedures and run test sessions for others.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work from the specification and the WPS
Find the WPS for a joint, read every detail, and follow it exactly.
Explain the WPS, PQR and WPQ, what each test involves and what a qualification covers.
Set up safely to the WPS
Set up and check the gas equipment, choose the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart, and set the flame the WPS names.
Choose and care for filler rods
Read AWS rod classes and keep rods clean, dry and identified.
Prepare, clean, gap, align, tack and mark plate and pipe coupons.
Weld plate in 1G to 4G and small-bore pipe in 2G, 5G and 6G, with the technique the WPS gives.
Inspect coupons by eye, prepare and judge face, root and side bends, and understand tensile, macro and nick-break tests.
Keep records and run a fair test
Record real values and results, issue WPQs, keep continuity logs, and run a test day fairly and safely.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the specification and WPS, qualification, gases, equipment, filler rods, flames, preparation, positions, technique, testing, defects, records, safety and calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practicals**: vertical-up (3G) plate coupons welded to a WPS, inspected, bend tested and recorded on draft WPQs; and small-bore pipe coupons in the 6G position, with a PQR-style record of the real values used.

blocks.note: The words matter in this unit: WPS, PQR, WPQ, continuity log, face bend, root bend, essential variable. Learn exactly what each one means.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working to an AWS specification: WPS, PQR and WPQ

blocks.p: When a client says a line or a tank must be welded "to the AWS code the Centre uses", it means three things: the welds are made to a **qualified procedure**, by **qualified welders**, and both can be **proved on paper**.

head: Document
What it is
What it proves
rows: The written method for a joint: base metal and thickness range, joint design, rod, gas, flame, nozzle, position, technique and any preheat
Nothing on its own: it is the instruction
The record of a test coupon welded to a draft WPS: the **real values** used and the results of the tests
That the method makes sound welds
The record of a welder's test: who, what was welded, the results, and the range now covered
That this person can follow the WPS and make sound welds

blocks.note: One test proves the **method**; the other proves the **person**. A good WPS in the hands of an unqualified welder, or a skilled welder working without a WPS, does not meet the specification.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: A draft WPS is written for the job
A competent welder welds a test coupon to the draft, while a recorder writes down every real value: base metal, thickness, rod class and size, nozzle, pressures, flame, position, technique, times
The coupon is inspected by eye, then tested, usually with tensile tests across the weld and face and root bends
The real values and the results go on the PQR, which is signed
If the tests pass, the WPS is finalised from the PQR, within the ranges the code allows, and approved for use
If they fail, the cause is found, the draft is changed and a new coupon is tested

blocks.p: Under most AWS codes, the welder who welds a PQR coupon that passes is also qualified as a welder, within the limits the code sets for that test. A WPQ is still filled in for that welder.

Some details of a WPS are **essential variables**: changing one changes the weld so much that the procedure must be tested again. Others can be changed by revising the WPS, but only by the person responsible, in writing. A welder never changes either kind on his own.

head: Usually essential (needs a new procedure test)
Usually changed by revising the WPS (follow the code)
rows: Fuel gas (for example acetylene to another gas)
Joint details such as the gap, within limits
Another rod class in the same filler group, where the code allows

blocks.note: Which changes are essential depends on the code and its tables. If you are not sure whether a change is allowed, the answer is to stop and ask, not to try it and see.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The **process** tested (OFW does not cover MMAW or GTAW).
The **positions**: a 3G plate test generally covers flat, horizontal and vertical; a 3G and 4G pair covers all positions on plate; a 6G pipe test generally covers all positions.
A **thickness range** and, for pipe, a **diameter range**, from the code's tables.
The **base metal and filler** groups tested.
**Pipe and plate:** a pipe test generally covers plate too, but a plate test covers pipe only above a large diameter set by the code. Small-bore pipe needs a pipe test.

**Continuity:** the qualification stays in force only while the welder keeps using the process, often with no gap longer than six months, shown on a **continuity log**. After a longer gap the welder must re-qualify.

blocks.p: A WPS has a number and a **revision** letter or number. Only the current, approved revision may be used. When a new revision is issued, the old copies are taken out of the bays, so no one welds to a superseded method. On drawings, the WPS number is often written in the **tail** of the welding symbol, with the process (for example "OFW WPS-07").

sections.title: Safety in the gas welding test bay

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Chained upright on trolleys or a wall, away from heat
Acetylene cylinders stood upright for the time the supplier gives before use
Spares kept in a ventilated store outside, oxygen apart from fuel gases by a safe distance (often about 6 m) or a fire-resisting wall
Checked every session: regulators, gauges, hoses, flashback arrestors at the regulators, check valves at the torch
Faulty parts tagged and taken out of use
Oxygen makes clothing and oily materials burn fiercely
Never use oxygen to freshen the air, cool yourself or blow off dust
Steel or firebrick benches; floor clear of rubbish and oil
Extinguisher close; fire check at the end of the session
Good ventilation or extraction in a closed bay: the flame makes carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides and uses up oxygen
Gas welding goggles of the right shade (about 4–6), flame-resistant clothing, gloves, boots
A cap and full cover when welding under a pipe coupon
Hot coupons handled with tongs and marked HOT, cooled in the place the assessor sets
Used only by the assessor or under direct supervision
Guards on; stand clear of the jig; eye protection

ul: Open the **oxygen** cylinder valve slowly, then fully.
Open the **acetylene** valve only about ¾ to 1½ turns and **leave the key on the valve**, so it can be shut in a second if there is a fire or a flashback.
Stand to the side of the regulator, not in front of it, as you open a valve.

blocks.note: If a flashback arrestor has stopped a flashback, take it out of use. Many arrestors must be replaced, or checked and reset, as the maker says, before the set is used again. Record what happened.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Gases, equipment and settings to a WPS

blocks.p: Fusion welding steel needs a flame hot enough, and concentrated enough, to melt a small pool quickly before the heat spreads. The oxy-acetylene flame is the hottest of the common fuel gas flames (about 3 100–3 200 °C at the tip of the inner cone), with most of its heat in that small cone. Other fuel gases are useful, but not for fusion welding steel.

head: Fuel gas with oxygen
Flame
Good for
rows: Hottest; heat concentrated in the inner cone
Fusion welding steel; also cutting, heating and brazing
Lower temperature; much of its heat in the outer flame
Heating, preheating, cutting and brazing; not fusion welding steel

blocks.p: The fuel gas is an essential variable in most codes: an OFW procedure proved with acetylene does not cover another gas.

ul: The WPS gives a nozzle size (or a range). Find it on the **maker's chart** for the torch you are using, with the oxygen and acetylene pressures that go with it. Each maker numbers its nozzles differently, so read the chart; do not match nozzles by eye.
As a rough guide, small welding nozzles for 1–3 mm steel often run at about 0.15–0.3 bar on both gases, and larger nozzles for 5–8 mm a little higher. Your chart is what counts.
Never set acetylene above about 1 bar (15 psi), or above the lower limit your supplier gives.
Clean nozzles only with the right tip cleaner. A damaged or enlarged nozzle gives a crooked flame and backfires; replace it.

head: Flame
How it looks
Effect on carbon steel
rows: Clear, rounded inner cone; the white feather has **just** disappeared
Clean, quiet, fluid pool; adds nothing to the weld. Named on almost every carbon steel OFW WPS
White feather round the inner cone
Adds carbon: the pool boils; the weld turns hard and brittle
Short, sharp, pointed cone; harsh hiss
Burns the steel: sparks, foam, porosity, brittle weld

blocks.p: That is why the WPS names the flame as well as the nozzle: the nozzle sets how much heat, but the flame decides whether carbon or oxygen gets into the weld. Check the flame during the weld; if a feather appears, add a little oxygen to bring it back to neutral.

ul: Hold the tip of the inner cone about **1.5–3 mm** from the pool. If the cone touches the pool, it backfires, pops and dirties the pool; if it is held far away, the outer envelope no longer shields the pool.
Keep the hot end of the rod **inside the outer envelope** between dips, so it does not oxidise in the air.

blocks.p: Steel gas welding rods are classified in the AWS filler metal specification with the letter **R** (rod) and a number. The number gives the **minimum tensile strength of the weld metal in thousands of psi (ksi)**.

head: Class
Minimum tensile strength
Typical use
rows: General mild steel work where strength is not critical
Carbon steel plate and pipe; the usual choice for carbon steel test coupons
Carbon and low-alloy steels needing more strength

blocks.note: To change ksi to MPa, multiply by about 6.9: 60 ksi × 6.9 ≈ 414 MPa. Use only the rod class the WPS names. Changing it is a change to the procedure that needs approval (and, under some codes, a new procedure test): an R60 procedure is not welded with R45 rod just because the store has run out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Too thick a rod chills the pool and gives poor fusion; too thin a rod melts off in drops before it reaches the pool, and the welder has to feed it so fast that he cannot watch the pool.

ul: Keep rods in their **labelled tube** or packet, dry and clean, until used. Rust, oil and dirt on a rod go into the pool and cause porosity.
Copper-coated rods have a thin coat that slows rusting; it does not make a dirty rod safe to use.
Each rod is stamped or tagged with its class. Keep classes apart, and never use an unmarked rod on coded work.
Record the rod class (and batch where required) on the test record.

blocks.p: Codes put base metals into **groups** with similar welding behaviour, so a test on one carbon steel covers others in its group. Check that the coupon plate or pipe is the grade the WPS names, and check the thickness: the procedure and the welder are both qualified only for a range of thickness.

sections.title: Joint preparation, fit-up and marking coupons

head: Coupon
Typical preparation (follow the WPS)
rows: **Square butt** with a small gap (for example 2–3 mm); the flame can fuse the full depth from one side
**Single-V**, about 60° included (30° on each plate), small root face, gap as the WPS gives; without a V the flame cannot fuse the full depth
Bevelled or square ends as the WPS gives, with a small gap; cleaned inside and out

blocks.note: The included angle is the **total** angle of the V. For a 60° single-V, each plate is bevelled at **30°**. Bevelling each plate at 60° gives a 120° groove that needs twice the filler and much more heat.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Grind or file the joint faces and about 25 mm each side, on **both** faces, to bright metal. Mill scale, rust, paint and oil cause porosity and stop fusion; the scale does not act as a flux.
Clean pipe ends **inside** as well as outside, so the root can fuse cleanly to the inside wall.
Remove burrs so the edges sit evenly.
Set the gap with a gauge and check it at both ends. A gap that is too wide gives burn-through and excess penetration; too small, and the root will not fuse through.
Check alignment: the code limits misalignment (hi-lo), because a step at the root stops full fusion and adds stress.
Tack each end with **small, fully fused tacks**. A big or cold tack leaves a lump and unfused metal inside the weld.
On pipe, place three or four small tacks round the joint, clear of the point where you will start.
Re-check the gap and alignment after tacking.

blocks.p: Before welding, the assessor marks each coupon with the welder's number or stamp, the test number and the position, and marks the top of pipe coupons. Marks go on the parent metal **clear of the weld and of the lines where bend strips will be cut**, as the code's coupon drawing shows. Marking first means coupons cannot be swapped, and every strip can be traced back to one welder.

sections.title: Welding technique in the test positions

head: Point
Forehand (leftward)
Backhand (rightward)
rows: Points ahead, onto the cold metal
Points back over the weld just made
Fed in front of the flame
Between the flame and the weld
Thin sheet, up to about 3 mm, where burn-through is the main risk
Plate over about 3 mm and pipe walls
Small, flat bead; preheats the joint ahead
Deeper fusion with a narrower V; the flame shields the hot weld; less rod and gas

blocks.p: The WPS names the technique because that is how the procedure was proved. Use the technique on the WPS in a test, even if you prefer the other.

head: AWS
ISO
Plate or pipe
rows: Horizontal groove on upright plate; pipe axis vertical

head: Position
Technique
Watch for
rows: Steady travel; full fusion of both edges and the root
Excess penetration if the gap is wide
Flame tipped slightly up; rod fed at the **upper** edge of the pool
Sag onto the lower plate; undercut on the upper
Start at the bottom; small pool melting both edges and the root; flame angled up so the pool sits on the weld below; rod at the front edge of the pool
Sagging pool; incomplete root at the start
Small pool, small nozzle within the WPS range, short quick dips of rod

ul: **2G** (axis vertical): weld round horizontally with the flame tipped slightly up; feed rod at the top of the pool.

**5G and 6G** (fixed): weld in **two halves**. Start just past the bottom centre and weld uphill on one side to just past the top. Weld the second half from the bottom, reheating the start of the first half and fusing into it, and finish by fusing into the end of the first half at the top.
Change your body position, torch angle and rod angle as you pass from overhead, through vertical, to flat.
The **bottom** (overhead) part is the hardest to fuse fully at the root: keep the pool small and make sure it melts through.
Do not turn or move a fixed coupon during the test: the position is part of what is being tested.
To restart after picking up a new rod, **reheat the end of the weld** until it melts, then fuse back into it before adding rod. A new pool started beside the old one leaves an unfused lap.
At the end of the run, **fill the crater** with rod and draw the flame away slowly, so it cools gently and does not crack.
Check both sides of the coupon when it is cool, before handing it in.

blocks.p: Every coupon is inspected by eye first. Only coupons that pass visual inspection go on to the bend or tensile tests. The acceptance limits come from the code the Centre uses; the figures below are typical examples.

head: Check
Typical requirement
rows: Complete fusion between weld and parent metal on the face and the root
Full, even penetration along the whole length; no incomplete fusion; excess penetration and concavity within the limits
No deeper than the code allows (often about 0.8–1 mm)
Within the code limit (often about 3 mm)

flow: Mark out strips across the weld from the places the code sets (on fixed pipe, so the overhead, vertical and flat parts are all tested)
Cut by saw or machine, not by flame near the weld: flame cutting heats and changes the metal
Grind or machine the face and root flush with the parent metal; round the long edges slightly
Mark each strip so it can be traced to the coupon and the welder
Bend in a guided bend jig round a former of the size the code gives
Examine the outside of the bend and measure any open defects

head: Strip
Surface stretched (on the outside)
Shows
rows: Lack of fusion at the cap and fill, especially at the toes; porosity near the face
Lack of root fusion or penetration
The whole cross-section, on its side
Faults through the full thickness; used on thicker coupons

blocks.p: Taking both a face and a root bend from a coupon tests both surfaces: a fault near the cap may not show in a root bend, and a root fault may not show in a face bend. Many codes reject a strip with any open defect longer than about 3 mm on the outside of the bend; smaller ones are accepted. Read the code for the exact limits and for how cracks at the corners are judged.

head: Test
How it is done
Pass
rows: A strip cut across the weld is pulled until it breaks; the load and the cross-section give the strength
Strength at least the code's minimum, usually the minimum strength of the plate. A break in the plate, away from the weld, at an acceptable strength shows the weld is the stronger part
A cut face is polished and etched
Full fusion and penetration; correct shape

ul: **Nick-break:** saw notches are cut in the weld and it is broken open. The broken face shows gas holes and unfused areas.
**Macro etch:** a section is cut, smoothed and etched with a mild acid, showing the outline of the weld, its fusion and its penetration.

head: Defect
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Gap too small; nozzle too small; travel too fast
Fit up to the WPS; correct nozzle; melt both root edges before adding rod
Lack of fusion at the toes (opens in a face bend)
Rod added before the edges melted; flame not playing on the edges
Melt each edge; pause at the sides
Dirty rod or plate; flame lifted off the pool
Clean to bright metal; keep the envelope over the pool
Reset to neutral and check it during the weld
Fill the crater; draw the flame away slowly
Gap too wide; nozzle too big; too slow

blocks.note: A failed strip fails the test. The welder may not pick a "better part" of the coupon for a new strip. A retest is allowed only as the code sets out, often after more training.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Records and running a qualification test

head: Record
What it holds
Why it matters
rows: Coupons cannot be swapped; strips are traced
The WPS used, and the real values: nozzle, pressures, rod, flame, position, times, stops
Shows the test followed the WPS
Each check and any faults, with sizes
Shows why a coupon went on to testing or failed
Each strip, its result and any defect sizes
The evidence for pass or fail
Welder, process, positions, base metal, thickness (and diameter) range, filler, results, witness, date, signature
Shows a client or inspector who may weld which joints
Dates each qualified welder used the process
Labelled and kept with the test records
Evidence if a result is questioned

flow: Weeks before: give each trainee the WPS and explain every detail; set practice coupons and bend some, so trainees see their faults and learn the limits
Before the day: check plates, rods, gas sets, arrestors, hoses, ventilation and the bend jig; book enough booths
On the day: brief the WPS, the test rules and the safety rules; issue marked coupons, the same materials and the same time to everyone
Watch fit-up and welding: the WPS, the position and the technique must be followed; you watch, you do not help
Each welder welds only his or her own coupon; no swapping, no finishing someone else's
Inspect every coupon by eye and record the result before any are cut
Cut, dress and bend strips from the set places, and judge them the same way for everyone
Record every result honestly, explain it to each trainee, and issue WPQs for passes

head: Sum
Example
rows: 10 trainees × 30 minutes each, in 2 booths: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 each × 30 = **150 minutes (2 h 30 min)**
A 200 mm coupon at 40 mm a minute: 200 ÷ 40 = **5 minutes**
4 torches × 150 litres an hour × 3 hours = **1 800 litres** of acetylene
80 litres of acetylene at J$5 = J$400, plus 90 litres of oxygen at J$2 = J$180: **J$580**
WPS 1.5–2.5 mm; measured 3.2 mm: **0.7 mm** over

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what OFW to AWS specification means, and the jobs of the WPS, PQR and WPQ.
I can describe how a procedure is proved and how a welder is qualified.
I can tell essential changes from those that only need a revised WPS, and I never change a WPS detail on my own.
I can say what a welder's qualification covers, including positions, thickness, pipe and plate, and continuity.
I can use only the current revision of a WPS and read a WPS number in a welding symbol's tail.
I can set up a safe test bay, open cylinders correctly and deal with a flashback arrestor after a flashback.
I can explain why acetylene is used for fusion welding steel and what other fuel gases are used for.
I can choose a nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart and set and hold a neutral flame.
I can read AWS rod classes such as R60, choose a rod size and keep rods clean and identified.
I can prepare, clean, gap, align, tack and mark plate and pipe coupons.
I can weld plate in 1G to 4G and small-bore pipe in 2G, 5G and 6G with fused restarts and tie-ins.
I can name the AWS and ISO positions.
I can inspect coupons and prepare and judge face, root and side bends.
I can explain tensile, macro and nick-break tests and judge results against limits.
I can keep test records and WPQs and run a fair test day.

terms: Record showing a welder has used a process within the set time
A test piece welded to show the quality of a procedure or a welder
A WPS detail that cannot be changed without a new procedure test
A bend test with the cap side on the outside of the bend
Welding with the flame pointing ahead and the rod in front (leftward)
Welding with the flame pointing back over the weld (rightward)
A jig that bends a test strip round a former of set size
The total angle of a V preparation
The small, bright cone of flame at the nozzle tip
A polished, etched section showing the weld's shape and fusion
A flame with no excess oxygen or acetylene
Breaking a notched weld to examine the broken face
AWS gas welding rod with a minimum weld metal strength of 60 ksi
Weld metal standing above the plate surface
A bend test with the root side on the outside of the bend
A bend test on a strip turned on its side, used on thicker coupons
Pulling a strip cut across the weld until it breaks

c1.title: Proving a procedure in Brown's Town
c1.text: A training centre in Brown's Town, St Ann, is proving a new OFW procedure for single-V butt joints in 8 mm carbon steel plate: 60° included angle, small root face, 2.5 mm gap, R60 rod, neutral flame, backhand technique, flat position. The instructor, Ricardo, welds the PQR coupon. Both transverse tensile strips break in the plate, well away from the weld, at 440 and 452 MPa; the plate's minimum is 400 MPa. Next week the store has no R60 rod, only R45.

c2.title: A test day in Porus
c2.text: Sophia is running an OFW 3G test day for six trainees at a centre in Porus, Manchester. In one booth she finds two copies of the WPS, revision B and revision C. One trainee's set had a flashback yesterday that the arrestor stopped. Each coupon uses about 90 litres of acetylene at J$5 a litre and 100 litres of oxygen at J$2 a litre.

c3.title: Bend results in Chapelton
c3.text: At a centre in Chapelton, Clarendon, the face and root bend strips from a group's 3 mm 3G plate coupons are laid out on a bench. On one face bend, a crack has opened along one edge of the cap, where the weld meets the plate. The root bends from the same coupons are sound.

c4.title: Welder records for a crew in Bath
c4.text: A crew from Bath, St Thomas, is to gas weld 60 mm outside-diameter carbon steel air lines in the fixed (5G) position at a factory. Odane's WPQ is for OFW on 3 mm carbon steel plate in the 3G position; his continuity log shows his last OFW work was eight months ago. To save money, the foreman suggests using oxy-propane sets for the job.

c5.title: Setting up the test bay in Claremont
c5.text: Before a test session at a centre in Claremont, St Ann, Tyrone is setting up four gas sets. A new trainee opens the acetylene cylinder valve several full turns and puts the key in his pocket. Spare oxygen and acetylene cylinders have been stood together in a corner of the bay.

questions.q: A trainee helping Ricardo bevels each plate edge at 60°. What should each bevel have been?
o: 30°, so the two bevels make a 60° V
60°, which matches the WPS figure
45°, the usual angle for gas welding
15°, as the gap gives the rest
questions.why: 60° is the included angle: the total angle of the V. Each plate is bevelled at half of it, 30°. Two 60° bevels make a 120° groove that needs about twice the rod and heat.

questions.q: What do the tensile results show?
o: The procedure fails: the strips should have broken in the weld
They pass: both broke in the plate above its minimum
Nothing yet: tensile results count only after bend tests
They fail: the two results differ by more than 10 MPa
questions.why: A strip that breaks in the parent plate, away from the weld, at or above the minimum shows the weld is stronger than the plate. Both strips exceed 400 MPa, so the tensile tests pass.

questions.q: The PQR coupon passes all its tests. What does that mean for Ricardo himself?
o: Nothing: he must still take a separate welder test before welding
He is qualified for every process and every position
He is also qualified as a welder, within that test's limits
He may weld only flat coupons for other procedure tests
questions.why: Under most AWS codes, the welder of a successful procedure coupon is also qualified as a welder within the limits that test covers. A WPQ is filled in to record it.

questions.q: With no R60 in the store, may the job be welded with R45 rod under this WPS?
o: Yes, as both are copper-coated mild steel gas welding rods
Yes, if the welder uses a slightly bigger nozzle with it
Yes, if the joints are bend tested afterwards to check
No: the WPS names R60; a change needs approval first
questions.why: The welder uses only the filler the WPS names. R45 is a lower-strength class than R60, so the welds would not be what the PQR proved. Changing the rod class means revising the WPS with approval, and under some codes a new procedure test.

questions.q: What should Sophia do about the two copies of the WPS?
o: Let each trainee choose whichever copy they find easier
Use the current approved revision and remove the old copy
Use revision B, as it was in the booth first
Keep both copies in the booth, since they are almost the same
questions.why: Only the current, approved revision may be used. A superseded copy left in a booth can lead someone to weld to an out-of-date method, so it is removed.

questions.q: Where should each trainee's coupon be marked?
o: Across the middle of the weld, where everyone can easily see it
On the back of the coupon, inside the root of the groove
On the parent metal, clear of the weld and the strip lines
On a paper label taped firmly to the face of the coupon
questions.why: Marks go on the parent metal where the code's coupon drawing shows, away from the weld and from where strips will be cut, so the marks survive and every strip stays traceable. A taped label can fall off or be swapped.

questions.q: What should happen to the set whose arrestor stopped a flashback yesterday?
o: Use it, because the arrestor worked exactly as it should
Use it after the hoses have been blown through with oxygen
Swap the arrestor onto the other regulator and carry on
Out of use until the arrestor is checked or replaced
questions.why: An arrestor that has stopped a flashback may be damaged or have its cut-off valve closed. It is checked or replaced as the maker says, and the event recorded, before the set is used.

questions.q: What is the total gas cost for the six coupons?
questions.why: Each coupon: 90 × J$5 = J$450 acetylene, plus 100 × J$2 = J$200 oxygen, so J$650. Six coupons: 6 × J$650 = J$3 900.

questions.q: What most likely caused the crack along the edge of the cap on the face bend?
o: Too much oxygen in the flame during the root run
The cap was not fused into the plate at that edge
The strip was bent the wrong way round in the jig
The root gap was set too wide for the plate
questions.why: A face bend stretches the cap side. A crack opening along a toe shows the weld metal lay against the plate edge without fusing, usually because rod was added before the edge melted.

questions.q: Why are both face bends and root bends taken from the coupons?
o: So that the strips can be shared between two trainees
Because one kind is used for practice and the other for the test
Each stretches a different surface, so faults at both show
So the welder can choose which result counts
questions.why: A face bend opens faults near the cap; a root bend opens faults at the root. Using both checks the whole weld.

questions.q: What does Odane's continuity log mean for this job?
o: He must re-qualify first: the gap is too long
He is still qualified, because his WPQ has no end date
He may weld if he practises on scrap first
He may weld the easy joints but not the overhead ones
questions.why: A qualification stays in force only while the welder keeps using the process, often with no gap over six months. Eight months without OFW means he must re-qualify.

questions.q: Even with an up-to-date log, would Odane's plate test cover the 60 mm pipe in 5G?
o: Yes: a 3G plate test covers every position on pipe
Yes: the pipe wall is about the same as his test plate
Only if he welds the pipe rolled instead of fixed
No: a plate test does not cover small-bore pipe
questions.why: A plate test covers pipe only above a large diameter set by the code. Small-bore pipe in a fixed position needs a pipe test, such as 5G or 6G.

questions.q: For which part of the job could oxy-propane sets be used?
o: Fusion welding the pipe joints, at a larger nozzle
Cutting and preheating, but not the fusion welds
The root runs only, with acetylene for the cap
Any of the work, as the fuel gas is not on the WPS
questions.why: Propane's flame is cooler and less concentrated, so it suits cutting, heating and brazing but not fusion welding steel. The fuel gas is also an essential variable: an acetylene procedure does not cover propane.

questions.q: How should the acetylene cylinder valve be opened?
o: About ¾ to 1½ turns, with the key left on the valve
Fully open, so that the gas flow is never restricted
Half a turn, with the key kept safely in the store
Fully open, then back a quarter turn, key removed
questions.why: A small opening gives enough flow, and a key left on the valve lets anyone shut it in a second in a fire or flashback. A valve opened many turns with the key in a pocket cannot be shut quickly.

questions.q: What should be done with the spare cylinders?
o: Leave them in the corner, chained together
Lay them on the floor so they cannot fall over
Store them outside, upright and secured, oxygen apart from fuel
Keep them beside the benches so empty ones can be swapped quickly
questions.why: Spare cylinders go to a ventilated store outside the bay, upright and secured, with oxygen kept apart from fuel gases by a safe distance or a fire-resisting wall, so a fire at one is not fed by the other.

questions.q: A trainee's 6 mm single-V coupon comes out bent upward along the weld, outside the alignment limit. What should he do on the next coupon?
o: Weld the root faster and the cap much more slowly
Use a bigger nozzle so the weld cools more evenly
Quench the coupon in water as soon as the cap is done
Preset the plates the other way before tacking
questions.why: A V weld shrinks most across its wide cap side, pulling the plates up. Setting them slightly the opposite way before tacking lets the shrinkage pull them flat. Quenching does not stop shrinkage, and a bigger nozzle adds heat and distortion.

questions.q: Six trainees each need 35 minutes in a booth to fit up and weld a coupon. There are two booths. How long will the session take, at least?
o: 1 h 45 min
3 h 30 min
35 min
1 h 10 min
questions.why: Two booths share six trainees: three each. 3 × 35 = 105 minutes = 1 h 45 min. One booth would take 3 h 30 min.

questions.q: A WPS for a 3 mm square butt coupon gives a gap of 1.5–2 mm. A trainee sets 3 mm. What is the likely result if he welds it like this?
o: Lack of root penetration along the whole joint length
Burn-through and too much penetration at the root
A carburised weld that turns hard and brittle in use
Lack of fusion at the toes of the cap on both sides
questions.why: Too wide a gap on thin plate lets the pool drop through, giving burn-through and excess penetration. The gap is reset to the WPS before tacking.

questions.q: A welder sets the acetylene to 1.5 bar "to get more heat", though the chart gives 0.3 bar. What is wrong?
o: Nothing wrong, as long as the oxygen pressure is raised to match
The higher pressure will turn the flame strongly carburising
It breaks the safe acetylene limit and the WPS settings
The higher pressure will freeze the regulator and the hose
questions.why: Free acetylene above about 1 bar can break down and explode. More heat comes from the right nozzle at the chart pressures, not from forcing a small nozzle.

questions.q: On a drawing, the tail of a welding symbol reads "OFW WPS-07". What does it tell the welder?
o: The weld is 7 mm in size and made on site
There are seven welds of this kind on the drawing
The welder must hold the seventh welder test
The process, and the procedure to weld it to
questions.why: The tail carries extra information, often the process and the procedure number. Here the joint is oxyfuel gas welded to WPS-07, which the welder must find and follow.
